detail.longDescription: For about the past six months, I feel that American society's views on AI have already fallen into a state of chaos. People say AI valuations are a bubble, AI can't produce effective productivity, AI companies aren't worth that much money, AI data centers are a waste of resources, and some even think the entire AI industry is just entertaining itself. But then a bunch of people can't live without AI. Seriously, if Anthropic and OpenAI were willing to sell themselves to China at what everyone calls "bubble valuations," China would be very willing to buy the entire AI bubble. Then, many people in the US don't want data centers, but they also don't want too many data centers to move outside the US. There's also another group of people saying Anthropic and OpenAI aren't open enough, believing these companies should open-source their models and shouldn't monopolize AI technology. Fine, then let's say Anthropic directly releases all the model weights, training methods, training data, and related technologies of Claude Opus 5.5 today. These people wouldn't be happy about that either. By then, issues like national security, cybersecurity, China's AI development, and technology leaks would probably all come up again. Besides, how many people can actually run these models? They would still need data centers. The same goes for GPUs. They don't want others to use them, but they don't want to pay for them themselves either. They want to pause AI development, but still hope to stay ahead, and hope their enemies won't develop it. Some people want everything to go back to how it was before, but also hope to make breakthroughs on many problems. Fine, pause technological development. Then a few months later, even if other "democratic" countries outside China develop it, they'll start talking about things like "industry loss," "national security," "unfair competition," and "how to bring the industry back to the US." Then they say things about safety and stopping, which all sound very nice, but everyone is accelerating development anyway. They say valuations are too high, then let them fall. But if they fall to 1/10, they're not happy either. When the industry is still in their own hands, they complain that it consumes too many resources, develops too fast, and has valuations that are too high. When the industry really ends up in someone else's hands, they start thinking this industry is extremely important to the country. You don't want it yourselves, so you give it away, and then cry about it after losing it. These opinions aren't necessarily coming from the same group of people, but all these internal disagreements are directly reflected in national policies, and directly turn the entire country into a mess. These policies contradict each other and fight against each other, with absolutely no consensus. It's like pressing the brake and accelerator as hard as possible at the same time. In the end, the engine will be destroyed, the brakes will break, and the car will overheat and catch fire. Sometimes I even wonder whether Americans will only have a more consistent view of AI after China's AI proves P = NP first. And finds a workable algorithm that makes a large number of passwords and cryptographic systems ineffective. Forget it, I think that's impossible. But I am genuinely looking forward to next January, when Americans take responsibility for their own choices and really pause all AI construction and development.
